items.title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
items.summary: Failures in deployed AI often stem from a mismatch between the task state and available context, which the paper terms context scaling. The effort to reduce this bottleneck is called context scaling, which is framed by three budgets: training ($B_\theta$), decision-time ($B_d$), and context-infrastructure ($B_c$). Context scaling specifically focuses on improving the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, and persist deployment state for model use. Effective-context value is defined based on task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separating deployment state from model-visible context. The research proposes an agenda focusing on grounded reporting, infrastructure, and safety for persistent AI systems.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling" details an investigation into the mismatch between task state and available context in deployed artificial intelligence systems, proposing a framework for improvement. The research introduces context scaling, which is defined by three budgets: training budget, decision-time budget, and context-infrastructure budget, focusing on enhancing the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, and persist deployment state for model use. Effective-context value is established through task- and intervention-dependent attribution, which distinguishes deployment state from model-visible context. The study advocates for an agenda centered on grounded reporting, infrastructure, and safety for persistent AI systems. This research signals a focus on foundational improvements necessary for reliable and scalable deployment of advanced artificial intelligence.

items.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
items.summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests AI models converge to a shared world representation across different modalities. This research investigates whether vision and language models also converge in how they operate on these representations, specifically focusing on the Jacobian-space (J-space). Evidence shows that the J-spaces of vision and language models converge approximately up to a rotation. Rotating a word's vector between modalities demonstrably changes the perceived object in vision or the output of image generation. This implies that models converge not only in representation but also in the actions taken upon that representation.

This story investigates whether vision and language models converge in how they operate on shared representations within the Jacobian-space. The research demonstrates that the Jacobian-spaces of vision and language models converge approximately up to a rotation. The study examined the relationship between vision and language models by analyzing the Jacobian-space transformations. Rotating a word's vector between modalities was observed to demonstrably alter the perceived object in vision or the output of image generation. This indicates that models converge not only in the representation space but also in the subsequent actions performed upon that representation. This finding suggests a deeper alignment between linguistic and visual understanding in artificial intelligence systems. Further investigation into cross-modal transformation remains a focus area for model development.

items.title: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
items.summary: Procedurally generated logic problems use planted proofs to evaluate and train reasoning in language models. The research measures the actual proof depth required for problems relative to stated depths and inference rules. Certificates are exported to verify the required steps, revealing what a problem truly necessitates. This method constructs problems where every proof has a requested structure, incorporating shortcuts. Training with these certified and mixed problem types improves model performance for Qwen3.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data" details a method for evaluating reasoning in language models by analyzing proof structures. The research measures the actual proof depth required for logic problems against stated depths and inference rules, demonstrating that certificates can be exported to verify the necessary steps. The methodology involved constructing problems where proofs incorporate specified structures and shortcuts, and these certified and mixed problem types were used for training to improve the performance of models like Qwen3. This approach reveals the true depth of reasoning required rather than the superficial stated depth. The findings suggest a pathway for more accurate and robust training data generation for advanced language models.

items.title: General-Purpose Decision Models for AI Configuration Tuning
items.summary: AI configuration tuning seeks optimal settings for AI performance within budget constraints, where the choice of decision strategy is critical. The research investigates whether general-purpose decision models can effectively guide this tuning process using a representative agent called Jev. Comparisons showed that conventional optimizers and predictors performed well, but region guidance led to configurations with lower perplexity. This approach provided quality gains when additional tuning time and fees were permitted. The findings suggest actionable advice for selecting decision roles and balancing tuning quality against cost.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "General-Purpose Decision Models for AI Configuration Tuning" investigates the use of general-purpose decision models to guide the process of optimizing artificial intelligence settings under budget constraints. Comparisons demonstrated that region guidance led to configurations with reduced perplexity, offering quality improvements when additional tuning time and fees were available. The research explored whether a representative agent named Jev could effectively direct the tuning process for AI performance. Conventional optimizers and predictors yielded satisfactory results, but the introduction of region guidance provided configurations exhibiting lower perplexity. This methodology suggests actionable guidance for selecting decision roles and balancing the quality of tuning against associated costs. The findings indicate a pathway for more cost-effective and high-quality AI configuration tuning in practice.

items.title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
items.summary: Large language model agents require reliable confidence scores to gate automated decisions, as LLMs can produce incorrect answers with high confidence. This work trains models using supervised learning to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers. A linear confidence score head fitted to the frozen LLM backbone is used to generate these scores. The proposed confidence scoring framework outperforms baselines for automating LLM-based agents with high accuracy. This method enhances the safety of automation by allowing uncertain outputs to be routed for human review.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models" reports on a method for ensuring the reliability of large language model agent decisions. The research introduces a framework for predicting the correctness of LLM-generated answers, demonstrating superior performance in automating these agents. The methodology involves training models using supervised learning to predict answer correctness. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the frozen large language model backbone to generate these scores. This approach was tested against existing baselines and showed improved accuracy in automating LLM-based agents. The framework allows uncertain outputs to be routed for human review, thereby enhancing the safety of automation processes. This work suggests a path toward more reliable and safer deployment of autonomous language model systems.

items.title: Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows
items.summary: Partial routing guides a lead model to delegate subtasks to cheaper worker models in agentic workflows. This is achieved by analyzing past runs to identify recurring subtasks and measure their quality and cost for each model. Delegation guidance is produced with a parameter $\delta$ controlling the delegation amount, allowing the lead to decide delegation dynamically. On benchmark tasks, partial routing achieved higher performance than using the lead alone or task-level routing. This demonstrates that analyzing past runs supports more efficient planning and delegation with minimal overhead.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Partial Routing: Trace-Tuned Delegation for Resource-Efficient Agentic Workflows" reports on a method for optimizing agentic workflows through partial routing. This research demonstrates that analyzing past execution data allows a lead model to effectively delegate subtasks to cheaper worker models in an agentic system. The methodology involves analyzing prior runs to identify recurring subtasks and quantify the quality and cost associated with executing those tasks across different models. Delegation guidance is formulated using a parameter delta, which permits dynamic control over the extent of delegation. Benchmarking on various tasks indicated that partial routing yielded superior performance compared to using the lead model exclusively or employing task-level routing. This suggests that incorporating historical run analysis facilitates more efficient planning and delegation with minimal computational overhead. Future developments in agentic systems will focus on refining such trace-tuned delegation strategies.

items.title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
items.summary: The research introduces a clinically grounded taxonomy for assessing harm in mental health contexts based on what, who, and when harm occurs. This framework separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, allowing for explicit, auditable safety policies. A reasoning-based guard model named MindGuard2 is trained using short reasoning traces and reinforcement learning to minimize inference overhead. MindGuard2 achieves competitive accuracy while significantly reducing latency compared to larger models. The work results in a safety guardrail model with state-of-the-art performance for mental health safety.

The research details the development of a reasoning-based guard model named MindGuard2, which was trained using short reasoning traces and reinforcement learning to minimize inference overhead. items.title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
items.summary: A study audited 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories regarding brand recall and category accuracy in language models. Category prompts elicited 510 brands, and a five-candidate probe ranked the reference label first for 787 brands. The overall error rate across separated rankings was 19.8%, which dropped to 3.5% for the best-performing brands. Measured brand recall varied across four Gemma generations, ranging from 39.8% to 51.1%. The findings suggest reporting brand recall and category accuracy separately is advisable.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands" details an audit of one thousand B2B SaaS brands concerning brand recall and category accuracy within language models. The study involved prompting five hundred and thirteen brands with category prompts, and a five-candidate probe was used to rank reference labels, with the reference label being ranked first for seven hundred eighty-seven brands. The overall error rate across separated rankings was nineteen point eight percent, which decreased to three point five percent for the top performing brands. Measured brand recall varied across four generations of Gemma models, ranging from thirty-nine point eight percent to fifty-one point one percent. Reporting brand recall and category accuracy separately is suggested by the findings. This research indicates that separate metrics for brand recall and category accuracy are advisable for assessing language model performance in business contexts.

items.title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
items.summary: A scoring framework is proposed to select the best candidate answers from LLMs and VLMs by combining hard and soft checks. This framework uses a drafting model, a configuring model, and scoring models to evaluate candidate properties. Application to tasks like code generation and QA showed that combining hard checks with candidate comparison significantly improves correctness and safety. The gain is largest when the initial sample is weak, with empirical improvements up to +0.28 for code safety. The method emphasizes grounded hard checks over soft-factor configuration for achieving performance gains.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection" details a scoring framework designed to select the best candidate answers from large language models and vision-language models by integrating hard and soft checks. This framework employs a drafting model, a configuring model, and scoring models to evaluate candidate properties. The application of this method to tasks such as code generation and question answering demonstrated that combining hard checks with candidate comparison significantly enhances correctness and safety. Empirical results indicate the greatest performance gains are observed when the initial sample is weak, yielding improvements of up to point two eight for code safety. The methodology prioritizes grounded hard checks over soft-factor configuration for maximizing performance. This advancement suggests a method for more reliable and safer candidate selection in generative AI systems.

items.title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics
items.summary: AutoformBench is a benchmark for evaluating AI systems on the task of formalizing advanced mathematics in Lean. It comprises 341 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. In these tasks, agents are given informal proofs and must construct the necessary definitions and supporting infrastructure in Lean. The benchmark assesses frontier models' ability to build this missing formal infrastructure. Performance results indicate that success depends more on constructing formal infrastructure than on specific mathematical domain knowledge.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics" details a benchmark designed to evaluate artificial intelligence systems on the task of formalizing advanced mathematics within the Lean proof assistant. Performance results indicate that success in this task relies more heavily on constructing formal infrastructure than on specific mathematical domain knowledge. The benchmark comprises three hundred forty one formalization tasks drawn from twenty four advanced mathematical sources. In these tasks, agents are provided informal proofs and are required to construct the necessary definitions and supporting infrastructure directly in the Lean environment. The evaluation assesses frontier models' capacity to build this missing formal infrastructure. Performance analysis suggests that the capability to construct the formal framework is a more significant factor than pre-existing mathematical expertise. This research points toward the importance of formal systems in guiding the development of mathematical artificial intelligence.
